statement: The draft is a good base: privilege changes, policy decisions, secret use and webhook authentication all have their own events. One thing in it would leak secrets, though. H1 asks EffectPermitted to carry the input as rewritten by the gate, and the network secrets gate in eyg_packages/cloud/secrets.eyg rewrites Fetch by putting the real secret value into headers, the path or the query. So the rewritten input must never be stored as it is. Also, granting privileges is spread across identity and configuration, so nobody can review in one place who can do what.

renames.why: Gates return Pass/Mock and execute.gleam records the decisions 'pass', 'mock', 'unavailable' and 'failed'. Using the same words in events and code avoids having two names for one thing.
'Replayed' sounds like a delivery we chose to run again, and runs.RunResumed already covers our own replays. This event means a duplicate or stale signed delivery was caught and refused.
Web shell cookies, HTTP API tokens and agent or connection credentials all need revoking. One event with a credential kind avoids a separate revocation event for each kind.

merges.why: Under the process boundary rule every process evaluates the configuration itself, so one event per read would flood the log. The evaluation event should list the name and version of each secret it read, which keeps secret use auditable without the volume.

splits.why: Erasure is a process that can be refused, for example under a legal hold, so the request must be recorded as well as the outcome. Destroying a subject's key (crypto-shredding events) is a different act from deleting blocks in the content store (files), and the two have different proofs.

missing.why: operation.gleam says the HTTP API can call every configuration operation, but nothing records who holds an API credential or which shell it carries.
A request with no recorded approval by a named second person is not reviewable. PersonShellAssigned should reference the approval.
Refused escalations matter as much as granted ones (denials recorded as carefully as passes).
When the channel shell's CID changed between the crash and the resume, the run continues with different privileges. That must be visible, along with the old and new CIDs (see H2).
Before recording, effect results, Posts and file writes should be scanned for known secret values and placeholders. Each redaction should be an event so leaks are found, not silently hidden.
Verifying a signature means nothing until we know whose keys a workspace trusts. That trust is a privilege grant and needs an event.
A compromised publishing key must stop verification from passing from a known position in the log onwards. Pinned releases signed before that point need a reviewable decision.
Sharing makes channel content public. Without a revocation event there is no way to tell when exposure ended.

context_changes.change: Split identity into 'identity' (authentication: CloudBootstrapped, PersonInvited, PersonSignedUp, PersonSignedIn, SignInRejected, ApiCredentialIssued, CredentialRevoked) and 'access' (grants: AdminGranted, AdminRevoked, ShellAssignmentRequested/Approved/Declined, PersonShellAssigned, WebShellBoundToChannel). Move configuration.ShellDefinitionPublished and configuration.ChannelShellChanged into 'access' too.
context_changes.why: A reviewer asking 'who can do what, and who changed it' should read one context. Today admin and person shells sit in identity while shell definitions and channel shells sit in configuration, though all four change capabilities. Configuration keeps the source versions. Access holds the capability facts derived from them.

hotspot_positions.position: Use separate events: EffectPassed, EffectMocked, EffectDenied and GateFailed. They have different payloads and different audit weight, and a reader can filter denials without decoding a field. Every one carries: run id, actor chain, effect label, the CID of the shell that decided, a digest of the requested input and (for passes) a digest of the input as executed. Never store the rewritten input verbatim: the secrets gate inserts the real secret into Fetch requests. Store the input as executed in redacted form (placeholders kept, secret names and versions listed), and emit SecretInjectedIntoRequest alongside it.

An EffectResultRecorded is a fact: on replay it is fed back without asking the gate again, because the world already changed. Any effect that was requested or decided but has no recorded result is decided again by the CURRENT shell. If the shell CID differs, emit ResumedUnderNewShell. If a secret was revoked or rotated, the injection uses the current version or is refused. A recorded Pass is never a standing permission.

Security view: never silently retry effects that are not idempotent and carry credentials, such as a Fetch with an injected secret or a Post. Reconcile with the platform where it offers delivery ids. Otherwise mark the effect in doubt and ask a person, and record their answer as an event naming who resolved it.

EffectMocked is its own event type, carrying the mocked value or its digest and the shell CID. EffectResultRecorded must reference the decision event it follows, so a projection can never show a mocked result as a real one. Mocked Env results for secret names hold placeholders. Today the placeholder is an unsalted SHA-256 of the secret value: see the new hot spot.

Use both approaches. Keep personal data out of event payloads where possible: store it as encrypted blobs referenced by CID, with keys per subject, or per channel for chat history. Events carry only references and digests. Erasure is ErasureRequested followed by SubjectKeyShredded, and the hash chain stays valid because only ciphertext is chained. Digests of personal data must be keyed (HMAC with the subject key) so they cannot be checked by guessing after the key is shredded.

Each stream is hash-chained. Signed checkpoints over the global order (AuditLogCheckpointSigned) are published at regular intervals and also exported outside the cloud, otherwise an admin with disk access could rewrite both the log and its seals.
Agree: upcast on read. Never re-encrypt or rewrite stored events, because that breaks the chain and erasure proofs.
Agree, traces cannot be the audit record. Decisions (pass, mock, denied, failed) are durable events. Traces can link to them by event id but must not be the only place a denial is recorded.

Effect inputs and results are classified per effect before recording. SetSecret's value is never recorded: the vault stores it and SecretSet records the name, version, actor and a keyed fingerprint. Env answers record the secret's name, not its placeholder. Fetch requests are recorded with placeholders, not values. Fetch responses and file contents go to encrypted blobs and are scanned (SecretLeakRedacted). A replay never needs the secret: the gate re-injects the current version on any new Fetch, and recorded results are fed back without one.

Agree, and go further: RunStarted or ReferencesPinned lists every resolved CID. Code fetched from the hub is hash-checked and its signature verified against a trusted signatory before evaluation. A run whose packages fail verification never starts, and PackageVerificationFailed is recorded.

Every event carries an actor chain: the root principal (a person, or a connection identified by its verified webhook or credential), then an agent, trigger, schedule or subagent delegated from it, each with the shell CID it held. An agent never acts with more than its principal's shell intersected with the channel shell.

CloudBootstrapped needs a one-time bootstrap secret given at startup, not 'the first visitor'. Sign-in goes through an external identity provider (OIDC, passkeys), and the event records the provider and verified subject. users.json tokens are stored hashed and expire, and are compared in constant time rather than with list.find and ==.

A runtime AddTrigger is a privilege-relevant event (TriggerAdded with actor chain, script CID and shell CID), because it gives a program a foothold that lasts beyond the session. Configured triggers win on a name clash. A runtime trigger never runs with a broader shell than the one in force when it was added; if the channel shell later narrows, the narrower one applies.

A Webhook with no secret must be an explicit opt-in recorded as UnauthenticatedConnectionCreated and flagged in views. Secrets passed as a query token are deprecated, because they leak into access logs and proxies. Use HMAC with a timestamp and delivery id, and a replay window that emits WebhookReplayDetected. WhatsApp's verify_token check uses plain ==; switch it to secure_compare. WebhookDeliveryAuthenticated records which method passed.

Rejected deliveries are always recorded, rate-limited and aggregated per source IP. Accepted high-volume deliveries may be stored as batched blobs by CID with one event per batch, but any delivery that matched a trigger and started a run must be individually addressable.

Security view: raw SQLite access outside dataclips is a privileged shell. Every DatabaseStatementExecuted records the actor chain and the dataclip or shell CID. Statement text may contain personal data, so it goes into an encrypted blob.

A revert is a new forward event, WorkspaceConfigurationReverted, pointing at the earlier source CID. It never removes history and never undoes effects already performed. A secret exposed by a reverted configuration must be rotated, not reverted.

new_hotspots.text: The network secret placeholder is 'eyg-secret-' plus an unsalted SHA-256 of the value (secrets.eyg). Any program, model provider or log that sees it can check guesses offline, and low-entropy secrets can be brute forced. Use an HMAC with a per-workspace key or a random handle, and never record placeholders in events.

The secrets gate adds 'authorization: Bearer <value>' to EVERY Fetch to an allowed host when no placeholder was used. A program can therefore use a credential without ever naming it. Should injection need an explicit placeholder, so each use is intended and can be audited?

An agent in a channel whose shell includes set_user_shell, set_workspace_source or set_secret can change privileges with no human in the loop. Should these commands require a human principal at the root of the actor chain, or a second approval, whatever the shell says?
A legal hold versus an erasure request on the same subject: which wins, and how is the refusal recorded and communicated?
